realExample.text: A confectionery maker reaches thousands of corner shops through wholesalers. Selling to each shop directly would cost more in order-taking and delivery than the shops are worth.

sections.misconception: Students describe the intermediaries as adding cost for nothing. They are paid for work the producer would otherwise do itself — holding stock, breaking bulk, reaching small buyers — and the question is whether they do it more cheaply than the producer could.
sections.examMatters: A Define (2 marks, WBS11 Appendix 6) requires you to define the term. A distribution channel is the route a product takes from producer to consumer — the definition is the route, not a list of the three types.

recall.prompt: Put the four stage channel into the order the specification names it, from the maker to the user:
why: The business that makes the product and sells it on in bulk
Buys in bulk and breaks it down, supplying many small retailers
Holds the stock a consumer can actually walk up to
The person who uses the product, and who pays the price every earlier stage has added to
recall.criterion: the order the product physically moves in

sections.title: Three Stage and Two Stage Channels
sections.keyIdea: Removing a stage gives the producer more of the price and more of the work, which is the trade every shorter channel makes.

body.text: The other two channels the specification names are the four stage one with stages taken out.

The **three stage** channel is **producer to retailer to consumer**. Zola sells to the retailer at $12, the retailer sells at $19.20, and Zola keeps $4 — double what the four stage channel left it. In exchange Zola deals with each retailer itself.

The **two stage** channel is **producer to consumer**: Zola sells direct, at $20, and keeps $12. Nobody else takes a share, and nobody else does any of the work either — the site, the payments, the delivery and the returns are all Zola's.

Set the three side by side and one thing stands out. The four stage and three stage channels both put the bottle in front of the consumer at **$19.20** — the same shelf price. What differs is how much of it reaches Zola: $2 against $4. The channel decision is rarely about what the consumer pays; it is about who does the work and who keeps the margin.

realExample.text: A furniture maker that sells through showrooms and also runs its own website earns very different amounts on the same sofa, and does very different amounts of work for each sale.

sections.misconception: Students write that a shorter channel means a lower price for the consumer. It means more of the price reaches the producer. Whether any of that is passed on is a separate decision, and often it is not.
sections.examMatters: A Calculate (4 marks, WBS11 Appendix 6) requires a calculation based on given data with workings given. Applying a mark-up at each stage in turn is that working, and the answer is the price at the end of the chain.

recall.prompt: Work the three stage channel through, from Zola's unit cost of $8:
template: Zola sells to the retailer at a 50% mark-up: ______
the retailer adds 60%, so the consumer pays ______
and Zola keeps, on each bottle: ______
hints: half as much again as the unit cost
the retailer's mark-up applied to what it paid
what Zola receives, less the $8 it cost to make

sections.title: Matching the Channel to the Product
sections.keyIdea: The right channel follows from what the product needs at the point of sale and how many buyers there are to reach, which is why a business often runs more than one.

body.text: No channel is best. Which one fits depends on three things about the product and its buyers:

items: **How many buyers, and how spread out.** A product bought by everyone needs the reach the longer channels give. A product bought by a few hundred businesses does not.
**What has to happen at the point of sale.** A product that needs explaining, fitting or demonstrating cannot be left to a shelf. One that sells itself can.
**What the margin will carry.** A long channel needs enough margin to pay every stage. A product with a thin margin cannot afford three sets of hands.

body.text: This is why businesses run several channels at once, and why the decision is properly a mix decision. Zola sells direct at $20 to buyers who come to it, and through retailers at $19.20 to buyers who would never have found it — and the two prices have to be close enough that neither insults the other.

That is the risk of multiple channels: a producer selling direct is competing with the retailers it also supplies. Price the direct channel too low and the retailers stop stocking it, which costs more reach than the direct sales were worth.

realExample.text: A shoe brand that opens its own online store while still supplying sports shops has to price carefully in both. The shops can see the website, and they have other brands to stock.

sections.misconception: Students write that selling direct is always better because the producer keeps more. It keeps more per sale and makes fewer sales, and it takes on work it may be worse at than the retailer was.
sections.examMatters: An Assess (10 marks, WBS11 Appendix 6) requires a well contextualised chain of reasoning, balanced and wide ranging, leading to a supported judgement. A channel decision is margin against reach, and the judgement says which matters more for this product.

recall.prompt: Sort each product by the channel it points towards.

groups.name: A longer channel
groups.why: Many buyers, spread widely, buying something that needs no explanation at the point of sale
items: A snack bought on impulse anywhere
A household battery
A bottled drink sold nationally

groups.name: A shorter channel
groups.why: Few buyers, or a sale that needs the producer present, or a margin that will not pay three sets of hands
items: A machine that must be installed and configured
A product sold to a few hundred businesses

sections.title: Changes in Distribution Methods
sections.keyIdea: Distribution has changed by making short channels possible at scale, which lets a producer reach buyers directly without the retail network it once needed.

body.text: The specification's last requirement in this topic is **changes in distribution methods**. The change that matters is that the two stage channel — producer straight to consumer — became practical for products and businesses it was never available to before.

items: **Selling online.** A producer can now reach buyers anywhere without a shop, which is what made the short channel possible at scale.
**Delivery instead of collection.** Once someone else will carry the product to the door, a producer does not need a network of places for buyers to walk into.
**Selling access rather than the object.** Some products are now supplied as an ongoing service — a subscription, a stream — so the distribution question becomes one of access.
**Several channels at once.** Most businesses now sell through more than one route and have to keep them from undercutting each other.

body.text: What has *not* happened is the disappearance of the longer channels. Retailers and wholesalers still do work the producer would otherwise pay for, and for a low-value product bought casually they do it more cheaply. The change widened the choice rather than settling it.
A short channel moves work as well as margin: a producer selling direct takes on the stock, the payments, the delivery and the returns.

realExample.text: A mattress maker selling directly to buyers online took on warehousing, delivery and returns that furniture shops had handled for a century. The margin came with the work attached.

sections.misconception: Students write that online selling has ended the need for retailers. Buying a chocolate bar through a producer's website would cost more in delivery than the bar — the longer channel still wins wherever the value is low and the buying is casual.
sections.examMatters: A Discuss (8 marks, WBS11 Appendix 6) requires logical chains of reasoning in context showing causes and effects, with a brief assessment showing awareness of competing arguments. The competing argument here is the work that moves with the margin.

recall.prompt: Match each change in distribution to what it allowed a producer to do:

pairs.left: Selling online
pairs.why: Removing the need for a physical place is what made the two stage channel workable at any scale

pairs.left: Delivery to the buyer
pairs.right: Stop needing places for buyers to walk into
pairs.why: Once the product travels to the buyer, the network of locations a retailer provided is no longer the only route

pairs.left: Supplying access rather than the object
pairs.why: A subscription or a stream is supplied continuously, so the distribution question stops being about moving a thing

distractors: Remove the need to hold stock

takeaway: The three channels are four stage, three stage and two stage, named for the stages on the route.
Both retail channels reach the consumer at $19.20; Zola keeps $2 or $4.
A shorter channel gives the producer more margin and more work, not the consumer a lower price.
Selling online made the two stage channel practical; longer ones still pay.

notes.title: Marketing Objectives and the Marketing Mix
notes.keyIdea: The specification names three marketing objectives — increase market share, increase revenue, building a brand — and they do not point at the same price.

items.text: Marketing objective — a measurable target a business sets for its marketing, with a deadline attached.
Market share — this business's sales as a percentage of the whole market's sales.
Revenue — price multiplied by quantity sold. Nothing is taken off it.
The concept of ‘marketing mix’ — the set of controllable decisions about product, promotion, price and place.
Increase market share — 60,000 ÷ 500,000 = 12%. It is relative, so sales can rise while share falls.
Increase revenue — $20 × 60,000 = $1,200,000. Revenue peaks at $16, not at the lowest price.
Building a brand — a longer-run objective that changes what the business can charge rather than what it sells today.
Product what it is · Promotion how buyers hear of it · Price what is charged · Place how it reaches them.
A decision in one constrains the other three — that is what makes it a mix rather than a list.
Asked to evaluate a marketing decision, say what the change forces in the other three elements. An answer that changes one and stops has described, not evaluated.

notes.title: The Product Life Cycle and the Portfolio
notes.keyIdea: The product life cycle and extension strategies describe one product over time; the Boston Matrix and the product portfolio describe all of them at once.

blocks.title: THE PRODUCT LIFE CYCLE AND EXTENSION STRATEGIES (1b)

items.text: Introduction sales from nothing, usually a loss · Growth sales climb · Maturity sales level, profit highest · Decline sales fall.
Profit lags sales, starts negative and peaks before sales do.
Extension strategies hold a product in maturity by changing one element of the mix — a new size, a new group of buyers, a new use, a new price, a new channel.

blocks.title: THE BOSTON MATRIX AND THE PRODUCT PORTFOLIO (1c)

items.text: Two axes: market growth up the side, market share across the bottom.
Question mark growing market, small share · Star growing, large · Cash cow flat, large · Dog flat, small.
The cash cow funds the question marks. A question mark that wins share becomes a star; a star in a settling market becomes the next cash cow.
A dog is not automatically divested. Say whether this one covers its costs, completes a range or holds a retailer relationship before recommending anything.
A Construct (4 marks) needs both axes labelled before any product is placed.

notes.title: Marketing Strategy and the Customer
notes.keyIdea: Marketing strategies appropriate for different types of market: mass markets, niche markets, business to business (B2B) and business to consumer (B2C).

blocks.title: MARKETING STRATEGIES FOR DIFFERENT TYPES OF MARKET (1e)

items.text: Mass markets — one standardised product for most buyers. Low unit cost from volume; competition on price.
Niche markets — a specialised product for a small group. Higher price and loyalty; a ceiling on sales and concentrated risk.
Business to business (B2B) — repeat orders in quantity, negotiated prices, a case that has to be justified to somebody else.
Business to consumer (B2C) — individual purchases, one published price, promotion to an audience the seller cannot name.

blocks.title: CONSUMER BEHAVIOUR: HOW BUSINESSES DEVELOP CUSTOMER LOYALTY (1f)

items.text: The product does what it promised → a problem is put right → the buyer is recognised → leaving would cost something.
A loyal buyer costs nothing to find, buys more often, and is less likely to leave over a price rise.
A niche is not automatically more profitable. Compare margin × volume, not margin alone.
Evaluating a loyalty scheme means asking what the business would have sold without it.

notes.title: Product and Service Design
notes.keyIdea: The design mix is function, aesthetics and cost/economic manufacture, and changes in the elements of the design mix to reflect social trends run through resource depletion and ethical sourcing.

items.text: Function — what the product has to do, and how reliably.
Aesthetics — how it looks, feels and sounds.
Cost/economic manufacture — whether it can be made at a cost that leaves a margin at the selling price.
The three trade against each other. Which one leads is a strategic choice, not a design one.
Concern over resource depletion: designing for waste minimisation, re-use and recycling — use less material, design the product to be used again, design so materials can be recovered.
Ethical sourcing — choosing suppliers on conditions and pay as well as price. Raises material cost; buys a claim, a buyer and a risk avoided.
Waste minimisation lowers cost by definition — less material bought, less thrown away. It is re-use and recycling that can cut either way.

notes.title: Promotion and Branding
notes.keyIdea: Types of promotion and types of branding, the benefits of strong branding, ways to build a brand, and changes in branding and promotion to reflect social trends.

blocks.title: TYPES OF PROMOTION (3a) AND TYPES OF BRANDING (3b)

items.text: Promotion — advertising (reach), sponsorship (association), social media (conversation), price promotions (immediate volume), direct contact (answers questions).
Branding — what the brand sits on (one product, or the whole range) and whose name it is (the maker's, or the seller's).
The specification lists no taxonomy for either, so the decisions are what is examinable, not a set of labels.
Added value — $20 less the $8 bought in = $12 a bottle.

Ability to charge premium prices — at $24 the unbranded line sells 40,000 bottles and makes $640,000 of profit; the branded one sells 48,000 and makes $768,000. Revenue is a different figure: $960,000 against $1,152,000.
Reduced price elasticity of demand — −1.67 before the brand, −1.00 after, at the same price and the same sales.

blocks.title: WAYS TO BUILD A BRAND (3d) AND CHANGES TO REFLECT SOCIAL TRENDS (3e)

items.text: Unique selling points (USPs)/differentiation — what there is to say. Advertising states it, sponsorship borrows an association, the use of social media lets buyers carry it.

Viral marketing — content made to be passed on; the spread cannot be bought. Social media — an audience built rather than purchased. Emotional branding — built on how the buyer feels, not on what the product does.
A strong brand need not sell more today. It loses fewer buyers when the price rises, which is worth more.
A low price is not a USP: any rival can match it by the end of the week.

notes.title: Pricing Strategies
notes.keyIdea: Types of pricing strategy, the factors that determine the most appropriate pricing strategy for a particular situation, and changes in pricing to reflect social trends.

items.text: Cost plus (mark-up on unit cost) — $8 at 50%/100%/150% gives $12/$16/$20.
Price skimming — launch high, come down as the buyers who pay most run out.
Penetration — launch low to win share, raise once buyers are established.
Predatory — below cost, to remove a rival. Restricted by competition law in many countries.
Competitive — at or near what rivals charge; the price is taken from the market rather than set.
Psychological — $19.99 to seem lower, or a round high price to signal quality.

blocks.title: FACTORS THAT DETERMINE THE MOST APPROPRIATE PRICING STRATEGY (4b)

items.text: Number of USPs/amount of differentiation · price elasticity of demand · level of competition in the business environment.
Strength of brand · stage in the product life cycle · costs and the need to make a profit.
All six are one question: how much room does this business have to set its own price?

blocks.title: CHANGES IN PRICING TO REFLECT SOCIAL TRENDS (4c)

items.text: Online sales and price comparison sites both cut the cost of comparing prices to almost nothing, which narrows the room and raises the value of everything that is not price.
Cost plus guarantees a margin on each sale made, not a profit. If the price is above what buyers pay, the margin is on nothing.
A Calculate (4 marks) requires workings. Show the mark-up applied to the unit cost, not just the price.

notes.title: Distribution
notes.keyIdea: Distribution channels — four stage, three stage and two stage — and changes in distribution methods.

items.text: Four stage: producer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer — $10 → $12 → $19.20. Zola keeps $2.
Three stage: producer to retailer to consumer — $12 → $19.20. Zola keeps $4.
Two stage: producer to consumer — $20 direct. Zola keeps $12, and does all the work.
The four stage and three stage channels reach the consumer at the same $19.20. What differs is how much of it reaches the producer.
Selling online · delivery instead of collection · supplying access rather than the object · several channels at once.
The longer channels have not disappeared: for a low-value product bought casually, a wholesaler and a retailer still do the work more cheaply than the producer could.
A shorter channel means more of the price reaches the producer, not a lower price for the consumer. Whether any is passed on is a separate decision.
A producer selling direct while supplying retailers is competing with its own stockists — price the direct channel carefully.

quiz.question: The marketing mix is best described as:
options: The decisions a business controls about product, promotion, price and place
The stages a product passes through from launch to withdrawal
The mix of customers a business sells to
The four types of market a business can sell into
quiz.explanation: The mix is the set of controllable decisions a business makes to sell a product. The stages from launch to withdrawal are the product life cycle, and the types of market are a separate requirement.

quiz.question: A strong brand is most valuable to a business because it:
options: Removes the need to advertise the product
Makes demand less sensitive to a change in price
Lowers the cost of making the product
Guarantees a larger number of sales each year
quiz.explanation: Reduced price elasticity of demand is the change a strong brand makes, and the ability to charge a premium price follows from it. A brand may sell the same number today and simply lose fewer of them when the price rises.

quiz.question: In a three stage distribution channel, the product passes from the producer to the:
options: Wholesaler, then to the consumer
Consumer directly
Retailer, then to the consumer
Wholesaler, then the retailer, then the consumer
quiz.explanation: A three stage channel is producer to retailer to consumer. Producer to consumer is two stage, and the chain through a wholesaler as well is four stage.

quiz.question: Which three marketing objectives does the specification name?
options: Increase market share, increase awareness, cut costs
Increase sales, build a brand, enter new markets
Increase profit, increase revenue, cut costs
Increase market share, increase revenue, building a brand
quiz.explanation: The three named objectives are increasing market share, increasing revenue and building a brand. Profit and cost are business objectives rather than marketing ones, and awareness is a means to an objective rather than one of them.

quiz.question: A business sells 60,000 units in a market where 500,000 units are bought in total. Its market share is:
quiz.explanation: Market share is the business's own sales divided by the whole market's, as a percentage: 60,000 ÷ 500,000 = 12%. The other figures come from dividing the wrong way round or from a different row of the schedule.

quiz.question: A business increases its sales for the year but its market share falls. This can only happen if:
options: Its costs rose faster than its sales
The whole market grew faster than its sales did
It sold to fewer customers than before
It cut its price during the year
quiz.explanation: Market share is relative, so it falls whenever the market grows faster than the business does. A price cut, a cost rise and the number of customers all say nothing on their own about what the rest of the market was doing.

quiz.question: Zola sells 100,000 bottles at $12 and 60,000 at $20. Its revenue at the two prices is:
options: Higher at $12
Higher at $20
The same at both
Impossible to compare without the cost
quiz.explanation: Revenue is price times quantity: $12 × 100,000 and $20 × 60,000 both give $1,200,000. The same revenue can come from a large number of cheap sales or a small number of dear ones, which is why revenue alone does not describe a business.

quiz.question: A business changes its product to a premium design but leaves its price, promotion and distribution unchanged. The main problem is that:
options: Market share will fall in the first year
The product life cycle will restart
The product will now cost more to make
The four elements of the mix no longer agree with each other
quiz.explanation: A mix works when a buyer meets the same message in all four elements. A premium product sold cheaply through the same channels tells the buyer two different things, and the mismatch itself is read as a reason to distrust the claim.

quiz.question: The four stages of the product life cycle, in order, are:
options: Introduction, growth, maturity, decline
Introduction, maturity, growth, decline
Launch, expansion, saturation, withdrawal
Growth, introduction, maturity, decline
quiz.explanation: A product is introduced, grows, matures and declines. Launch, expansion, saturation and withdrawal simply rename the stages, and the other two orders put growth and maturity the wrong way round.

quiz.question: On a product life cycle diagram, profit:
options: Rises and falls exactly with sales
Starts negative and peaks before sales do
Is highest at the moment of launch
Stays constant through maturity
quiz.explanation: Profit lags sales, starts below zero while launch spending is being recovered, and peaks in maturity before sales reach their own peak — because the price is falling by the time volume is highest.

quiz.question: A business sells a breakfast cereal to children and begins promoting the same cereal to adults as an evening snack. This is:
options: A change to the design mix
A new product launch
An extension strategy
A penetration pricing strategy
quiz.explanation: The product is unchanged and a new group of buyers has been found for it, which holds it in maturity rather than starting a new cycle. A new product would have its own introduction stage and its own launch spending to recover.

quiz.question: On the Boston Matrix, a product in a market that is growing quickly but where the business holds only a small share is:
options: A star
A cash cow
A dog
A question mark
quiz.explanation: High market growth with low market share is a question mark: the market is worth being in, and the business is not yet established in it, so cash is needed before the product says anything definite.

quiz.question: A business is considering withdrawing a product in the dog quadrant. Before deciding it should check whether the product:
options: Covers its own costs or completes a range a retailer stocks
Has a higher market share than any rival
Has ever been profitable in the past
Could be moved into a growing market
quiz.explanation: A dog is not automatically withdrawn. One that covers its costs, completes a range or holds a retailer relationship earns its place, and the matrix exists to inform that judgement rather than to make it.

quiz.question: Which of these is characteristic of a mass market strategy?
options: A specialised product at a higher price
A standardised product with a low unit cost from volume
Promotion aimed at one small group of buyers
A ceiling on how many units can be sold
quiz.explanation: A mass market sells one standard product to as many buyers as possible, which brings the unit cost down. A specialised product at a higher price, promotion aimed at one small group, and a ceiling on sales all describe a niche strategy instead.

quiz.question: A business argues that its niche strategy must be more profitable than a rival's mass market one because its margin on each sale is larger. This reasoning is:
options: Correct, because margin is what determines profit
Correct, because niche buyers are more loyal
Wrong, because profit is margin multiplied by volume
Wrong, because niche products always cost more to make
quiz.explanation: A wide margin on a small number of sales can earn less than a thin margin on a large number. The comparison is margin times volume, and loyalty and unit cost do not settle it either.

quiz.question: The most reliable difference between selling to a business and selling to a consumer is that a business purchase:
options: Involves a larger quantity than a consumer buys
Is settled by negotiating on price
Ignores how the product looks or feels
Usually has to be justified to somebody else
quiz.explanation: A business buyer typically answers to someone else, so the argument has to survive being repeated. Business buyers still have preferences, and larger orders and negotiated prices are common without being reliable.

quiz.question: A customer returns to a business only while a discount code is running. This shows that:
options: The business is paying for sales it may have had anyway
The product must be better than its rivals
The loyalty scheme is working as intended
The business has built genuine customer loyalty
quiz.explanation: A buyer who returns only while the discount lasts is buying a discount rather than showing loyalty, and the business may be paying for purchases that would have happened without it. Loyalty is built on the product working first.

quiz.question: The three elements of the design mix are:
options: Product, price and place in the marketing mix
Function, aesthetics and cost/economic manufacture
Quality, durability and the price charged
Design, materials and method of manufacture
quiz.explanation: The design mix is function, aesthetics and cost/economic manufacture. Product, price and place are three of the four elements of the marketing mix, which is a different requirement.

quiz.question: A business redesigns its packaging so that it uses less card and produces less offcut waste. The effect on cost is that it:
options: Cannot be determined without the sales figures
Rises, because sustainable design costs more
Falls, because less material is bought and less thrown away
Stays the same, because the product is unchanged
quiz.explanation: Waste minimisation lowers cost by definition: less material is bought and less is discarded in making it. Re-use and recycling are the responses that can move cost either way.

quiz.question: A luxury watchmaker chooses a hand-finished case that slows production. In design mix terms it has:
options: Improved cost at the expense of function
Improved all three at once
Improved function at the expense of aesthetics
Improved aesthetics at the expense of cost
quiz.explanation: A hand-finished case is an aesthetic decision paid for in cost and output. The design mix is one decision with three consequences, and moving towards one element is paid for at another.

quiz.question: A business that sources ethically finds no buyer mentions it. The spending has still bought it:
options: Protection against a supply scandal
A unique selling point by definition
A lower material cost
A guaranteed rise in market share
quiz.explanation: The value of a supply chain that has been examined shows up as the scandal that does not happen, which is real and invisible at once. Ethical sourcing raises the material cost, and it is a selling point only if buyers care about it.

quiz.question: A business wants promotion whose effect on sales it can measure exactly. It should choose:
options: A sponsorship of a local sports team
A discount code used at the checkout
A poster campaign across the city
A change to the product packaging
quiz.explanation: A code used at the checkout can be counted exactly. A sponsorship and a poster campaign reach people whose purchases cannot be traced back to them, and packaging is a product decision rather than a type of promotion.

quiz.question: A business puts one name on every product it sells. The main risk is that:
options: New products take longer to launch
Each product must be advertised separately
A problem with one product damages all the others
The products cannot be priced differently
quiz.explanation: A shared name carries a new product for free and carries a failure just as efficiently. Products under one name can still be priced separately and launch faster, which is the benefit being traded against the risk.

quiz.question: The three benefits of strong branding the specification names are:
options: Higher market share, higher revenue and higher profit each year
Advertising, sponsorship and the use of social media
Lower production costs, higher output and better product quality
Added value, the ability to charge premium prices, and reduced price elasticity of demand
quiz.explanation: Added value, premium prices and reduced price elasticity of demand are the specification's three. Advertising, sponsorship and social media are ways to BUILD a brand rather than benefits of having one, and the rest are outcomes that may or may not follow.

quiz.question: Which of these is most likely to work as a unique selling point?
options: A lifetime guarantee honoured without a receipt
A large advertising budget behind it
The lowest price on the shelf that week
A wide choice of colours across the range
quiz.explanation: A selling point holds only if copying it would cost a rival something real. A price can be matched by the end of the week at no cost but margin, colours are easy to add, and an advertising budget is not a feature of the product.

quiz.question: A business says it will "make its next campaign go viral". The problem with this plan is that:
options: Viral marketing is more expensive than advertising
Whether content spreads is decided by the people who see it
Viral marketing only works for products aimed at young buyers
Social media cannot be measured
quiz.explanation: A business can make something worth sharing; it cannot make it spread. That is why viral reach is planned for as a possibility rather than as a budget line.

quiz.question: A business has a unit cost of $8 and applies a mark-up of 100%. Its price is:
quiz.explanation: Cost plus is the unit cost multiplied by one plus the mark-up: $8 × 2 = $16. The other prices come from the 50% and 150% mark-ups, or from adding no mark-up at all.

quiz.question: A business launches a product at a high price and lowers it in steps over the following two years. This is:
options: Psychological pricing
Penetration pricing
Predatory pricing
Price skimming
quiz.explanation: Skimming launches high to take the buyers who will pay most and comes down as they run out. Penetration is the mirror image, starting low to win share.

quiz.question: What distinguishes predatory pricing from simply charging a low price?
options: The price is set below the cost of production to remove a rival
The price is lower than every competitor charges
The price is only offered to new customers
The price ends in .99 to look smaller
quiz.explanation: Predatory pricing is a loss taken deliberately to make the market unprofitable for a rival. A low price from a business with genuinely lower costs is competition working, not predation.

quiz.question: A business prices a product at $19.99 rather than $20. It is relying on the fact that:
options: The cost of production has fallen by one cent
Buyers read the first digit before the rest
A lower price always raises revenue
Rivals cannot match a price ending in .99
quiz.explanation: Psychological pricing changes how large the price seems rather than how large it is. The same strategy works in reverse: a round, high price signals that the business is not competing on price.

quiz.question: Which of these is one of the six factors the specification names as determining the most appropriate pricing strategy?
options: The number of people the business employs
The age of the business in years
Stage in the product life cycle
The legal structure the business has chosen
quiz.explanation: The six are the number of USPs or amount of differentiation, price elasticity of demand, the level of competition in the business environment, the strength of brand, the stage in the product life cycle, and costs and the need to make a profit.

quiz.question: A four stage distribution channel runs:
options: Producer to consumer to retailer
Wholesaler to producer to retailer to consumer
Producer to retailer to wholesaler to consumer
Producer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer
quiz.explanation: The specification's wording is producer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer. The wholesaler buys in bulk and breaks it down for retailers, so it comes before the retailer in the chain.

quiz.question: Zola can sell to a retailer at $12, who sells at $19.20, or through a wholesaler and a retailer who also reach the consumer at $19.20. The difference between the two channels is:
options: How much of the price reaches Zola
The quality of the bottle
How quickly the bottle is delivered
What the consumer pays
quiz.explanation: The consumer pays $19.20 either way. What differs is how much reaches the producer: $4 through the shorter chain against $2 through the longer one.

quiz.question: A producer that starts selling directly to consumers online will:
options: Always be able to charge a lower price
Keep more of each sale and take on more of the work
No longer need to hold any stock
Reach more buyers than through retailers
quiz.explanation: A shorter channel gives the producer more of the price and the stock, payments, delivery and returns that the retailer used to absorb. Whether any of the margin is passed on is a separate decision, and reach usually falls rather than rises.

practice.question: Define the term 'marketing objective'. (2 marks)
practice.guidance: Two things in one sentence: a target a business sets for its marketing, stated so that it can be measured. A definition with only the first half — "something the marketing is trying to do" — leaves out what separates an objective from a wish. An example is application and belongs in a 4-mark Explain; Define carries 2 marks in IAL Business (WBS11 Appendix 6).

practice.question: A business sells 60,000 bottles in a year. The whole market buys 500,000 bottles. Calculate its market share, and calculate its revenue if each bottle sells for $20. (4 marks)
practice.guidance: Show both workings. Market share = 60,000 ÷ 500,000 × 100 = 12%. Revenue = $20 × 60,000 = $1,200,000. Divide the business's own sales by the whole market's, not the other way round, and keep revenue as price times quantity with nothing taken off it — costs belong to a different calculation. Workings should be given for a Calculate (WBS11 Appendix 6).

practice.question: Construct a product life cycle diagram for a product now in maturity, showing both sales and profit and marking where an extension strategy would be applied. (4 marks)
practice.guidance: Construct requires an accurately labelled diagram (WBS11 Appendix 6), so the labels are the answer rather than decoration. The diagram needs: time on the horizontal axis and sales/profit on the vertical, both labelled; the four stages marked and named — introduction, growth, maturity, decline; a sales curve rising then falling; a separate profit curve that starts BELOW the axis, crosses it during growth and peaks before sales do; and the extension applied at the point where sales begin to level off, drawn as the sales curve being held up rather than as a second curve starting from nothing.

practice.question: Discuss whether a business entering the reusable bottle market should adopt a niche strategy rather than a mass market one. (8 marks)
practice.guidance: Levels-marked: the quality of the chain from knowledge to application to analysis decides the level, not the number of points made. Knowledge: a niche serves a small group whose needs the standard product misses; a mass market sells one standardised product to as many buyers as possible. Application: use the business in the extract — its size, its product, its rivals. Analysis: the niche allows a higher price because buyers are not choosing on price, and a wider margin on each sale; the mass market brings the unit cost down through volume. Then weigh the limits — the niche has a ceiling on sales and concentrated risk if tastes move or a larger rival enters, and the mass market means competing on price against businesses with lower costs. A Discuss requires a brief assessment showing awareness of competing arguments (WBS11 Appendix 6), so end with which fits THIS business and why.

practice.question: Explain one way in which improving the aesthetics of a product may affect the other two elements of the design mix. (4 marks)
practice.guidance: One way, explained with a reason and a detail — not a list of three. A hand-finished case improves aesthetics; it takes longer to produce, so the cost of making each unit rises, which is the cost/economic manufacture element moving in response. It may also affect function: a finish chosen for its look can be less hard-wearing than one chosen for durability. Explain requires a brief explanation of cause or effect supported by details or examples (WBS11 Appendix 6), and the cause here is the trade-off, not the decision.

practice.question: Assess whether building a strong brand is the best use of a marketing budget for a business selling reusable bottles. (10 marks)
practice.guidance: Levels-marked and judged on the chain, not on the number of points. Knowledge: the three benefits of strong branding are added value, the ability to charge premium prices and reduced price elasticity of demand. Application: use the business's own figures from the extract. Analysis: a brand that makes demand less price sensitive lets the business hold a price rise it could not otherwise hold — $640,000 against $768,000 at the same price, on this section's figures — which is worth more than the extra volume a discount would buy. Then assess the other side: brand spending is certain and immediate while the return is later and uncertain; the same money spent on distribution reaches buyers who have never seen the product; and a brand built on how buyers feel is damaged by things that have nothing to do with the product. Assess requires balanced, wide-ranging assessment leading to a supported judgement (WBS11 Appendix 6), so name the condition under which the answer changes.

practice.question: Evaluate which pricing strategy a business should adopt when launching a reusable bottle into a market where several established rivals already sell a similar product. (20 marks)
practice.guidance: Levels-marked and judged on the weighing. Build the case for each candidate against the six factors the specification names — the number of USPs or amount of differentiation, price elasticity of demand, the level of competition in the business environment, the strength of brand, the stage in the product life cycle, and costs and the need to make a profit. Several established rivals with a similar product means little differentiation, a weak brand at launch and price elastic demand, which points away from skimming: there is nothing rivals cannot match, so a high price invites them to undercut it rather than rewarding the early buyer. Penetration fits the conditions but is hard to reverse, because buyers recruited by a low price are the ones most likely to leave when it rises. Competitive pricing is the honest reading of a crowded market and concedes the initiative. Cost plus guarantees a margin on each sale and ignores whether the sale happens. Then take it further: the pricing decision cannot be made alone, because a price only holds if the product, promotion and distribution support it, and the real recommendation may be to build a selling point before launching at all. Evaluate requires a perceptive conclusion proposing a solution or recommendation (WBS11 Appendix 6) — supporting one from the extract rather than restating the options is what separates the top level.

practice.question: A producer can reach consumers at $19.20 through a retailer, keeping $4 a unit, or sell directly at $20 and keep $12. Analyse the factors the producer should consider before choosing to sell directly. (6 marks)
practice.guidance: Developed reasoning rather than a list, and no evaluation is required. Start from what the figures say: selling directly keeps $12 a unit against $4, which is more of the price on every sale made. Then take it somewhere. The retailer was doing work the producer now takes on — holding stock, taking payment, delivering, handling returns — so the extra margin arrives with costs attached. Reach falls, because a retailer's shelf is seen by buyers who will never visit the producer's site. And a producer selling directly while still supplying retailers is competing with its own stockists, who can drop the product. Analyse requires a brief chain of reasoning and includes interpretation where it is applied to given data (WBS11 Appendix 6), so use both figures rather than quoting one.

flashcards.front: Name the three marketing objectives the specification lists.
flashcards.back: Increase market share; increase revenue; building a brand. They are separate targets and they do not point at the same price.

flashcards.front: How is market share calculated?
flashcards.back: The business's own sales divided by the whole market's sales, as a percentage. It is a relative measure, so sales can rise while share falls if the market grew faster.

flashcards.front: What is revenue, and how does it differ from market share?
flashcards.back: Revenue is price × quantity. Market share is largest at the lowest price; revenue rises to a peak and falls again, so the two objectives set different prices.

flashcards.front: What is the marketing mix?
flashcards.back: The set of decisions a business controls: product, promotion, price and place. A decision in one constrains the other three — which is why it is a mix and not a list.

flashcards.front: Name the four stages of the product life cycle.
flashcards.back: Introduction — sales from nothing, usually a loss. Growth — sales climb. Maturity — sales level off, profit highest. Decline — sales fall away.

flashcards.front: Why is the profit curve not the same shape as the sales curve?
flashcards.back: Profit lags sales: it starts negative while launch spending is recovered, crosses zero in growth, and peaks before sales do, because the price is falling by the time volume is highest.

flashcards.front: What is an extension strategy?
flashcards.back: A change to one element of the mix that holds a product in maturity for longer — a new size, a new group of buyers, a new use, a new price, a new channel. It does not start a new life cycle.

flashcards.front: What are the two axes of the Boston Matrix?
flashcards.back: Market growth up the side and market share across the bottom. Both are about the market, not about how much the business sells.

flashcards.front: Name the four quadrants of the Boston Matrix.
flashcards.back: Star (growing market, large share) · Question mark (growing, small) · Cash cow (flat, large) · Dog (flat, small).

flashcards.front: How is a product portfolio managed?
flashcards.back: By cash. The cash cow needs little spending and funds the question marks; a question mark that wins share becomes a star, and a star whose market settles becomes the next cash cow.

flashcards.front: Should a dog always be withdrawn?
flashcards.back: No. A dog that covers its own costs, completes a range a retailer stocks, or matters to buyers the business wants to keep earns its place. The matrix informs the judgement rather than making it.

flashcards.front: Name the four types of market the specification lists for marketing strategy.
flashcards.back: Mass markets, niche markets, business to business (B2B) and business to consumer (B2C).

flashcards.front: What are the advantages and limits of a mass market strategy?
flashcards.back: A standardised product in high volume brings the unit cost down. The market is crowded and buyers compare on price, which is the one thing a business with nothing to distinguish it least wants to compete on.

flashcards.front: What are the advantages and limits of a niche strategy?
flashcards.back: Buyers choose it for what the standard product does not do, so the price holds and the margin is wider. Against that: a ceiling on sales, and concentrated risk if tastes move or a larger rival enters.

flashcards.front: What is the most reliable difference between B2B and B2C?
flashcards.back: A B2B purchase is usually justified to somebody else, so the argument has to survive being repeated — which is why it turns on cost, reliability and terms. A consumer answers to nobody.

flashcards.front: How do businesses develop customer loyalty?
flashcards.back: The product does what it promised → a problem is put right when it happens → the returning buyer is recognised → leaving would cost something. A scheme belongs at the third step and cannot substitute for the first.

flashcards.front: Why is a loyal customer worth more than the discount that bought them?
flashcards.back: They cost nothing to find, buy more often, and are less likely to leave over a price rise. A buyer who returns only while a discount runs is buying the discount, not showing loyalty.

flashcards.front: Name the three elements of the design mix.
flashcards.back: Function — what it must do. Aesthetics — how it looks and feels. Cost/economic manufacture — whether it can be made at a cost that leaves a margin.

flashcards.front: Why is the design mix a trade-off?
flashcards.back: Improving one element is paid for at another: a better finish costs output, a wider lid costs sealing. Which element leads is a strategic choice — budget leads on cost, luxury on aesthetics, safety equipment on function.

flashcards.front: How does concern over resource depletion change the design mix?
flashcards.back: Through waste minimisation (use less material), re-use (design it to be used again) and recycling (design so materials can be recovered). Recyclability becomes a function requirement the product did not have.

flashcards.front: Does designing for the environment always raise costs?
flashcards.back: No. Waste minimisation lowers cost by definition — less material bought, less thrown away. It is re-use and recycling that can move cost either way, and ethical sourcing that reliably raises it.

flashcards.front: What is ethical sourcing, and what does the extra cost buy?
flashcards.back: Choosing suppliers on conditions and pay as well as price. It buys a claim the business can honestly make, a buyer who chose it for that reason, and a supply scandal that does not happen.

flashcards.front: Name the main types of promotion and what each one buys.
flashcards.back: Advertising — reach. Sponsorship — association. Social media — conversation. Price promotions — immediate volume. Direct contact — the only type that can answer a question.

flashcards.front: What two questions separate the types of branding?
flashcards.back: What the brand sits on — one product, or the whole range — and whose name it is: the maker's, or the seller's. A shared name carries a new product for free and carries a failure just as efficiently.

flashcards.front: Name the three benefits of strong branding.
flashcards.back: Added value; the ability to charge premium prices; reduced price elasticity of demand. The third is the change, and the first two follow from it.

flashcards.front: What does a strong brand actually change about demand?
flashcards.back: Not its level — its sensitivity to price. On this section's figures, price elasticity at $20 moves from −1.67 to −1.00, and the profit-maximising price moves from $20 to $24.

flashcards.front: What is added value?
flashcards.back: The selling price less what was bought in to make the product. At $20 a bottle costing $8 to make, the value added is $12.

flashcards.front: Name the four ways to build a brand the specification lists.
flashcards.back: Unique selling points (USPs)/differentiation; advertising; sponsorship; the use of social media. USPs come first because they are what there is to say.

flashcards.front: What makes something a genuine USP?
flashcards.back: That copying it would cost a rival something real. A low price is not a USP: any rival can match it by the end of the week for nothing but margin.

flashcards.front: How do advertising, sponsorship and social media differ?
flashcards.back: Advertising states the claim with total control. Sponsorship borrows an association and makes no claim. Social media lets buyers carry it — the least control and the most credibility.

flashcards.front: Name the three changes in branding and promotion to reflect social trends.
flashcards.back: Viral marketing — content made to be passed on. Social media — an audience built rather than bought. Emotional branding — built on how the buyer feels, not on what the product does.

flashcards.front: Can a business make a campaign go viral?
flashcards.back: It can make something worth sharing. Whether it spreads is decided by the people who see it, so viral reach is planned for as a possibility and never as a budget line.

flashcards.front: Name the six types of pricing strategy.
flashcards.back: Cost plus (mark-up on unit cost) · price skimming · penetration · predatory · competitive · psychological.

flashcards.front: How is a cost plus price calculated?
flashcards.back: Unit cost × (1 + mark-up). $8 at 50%, 100% and 150% gives $12, $16 and $20. Nothing in it looks at the buyer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between skimming and penetration?
flashcards.back: Skimming launches high and comes down as the buyers who pay most run out; penetration launches low to win share and raises the price later. Skimming invites rivals in; penetration is hard to reverse.

flashcards.front: What makes pricing predatory rather than just low?
flashcards.back: The price is set below cost, deliberately, to make the market unprofitable for a rival until it leaves. A low price from genuinely lower costs is competition working. Predatory pricing is restricted by competition law in many countries.

flashcards.front: Name the six factors that determine the most appropriate pricing strategy.
flashcards.back: Number of USPs/amount of differentiation · price elasticity of demand · level of competition in the business environment · strength of brand · stage in the product life cycle · costs and the need to make a profit.

flashcards.front: What do online sales and price comparison sites change about pricing?
flashcards.back: They cut the cost of comparing prices to almost nothing, which raises price elasticity of demand and narrows the room every strategy depends on — and raises the value of everything a comparison site cannot sort on.

flashcards.front: Name the three distribution channels the specification lists.
flashcards.back: Four stage: producer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer. Three stage: producer to retailer to consumer. Two stage: producer to consumer.

flashcards.front: What does a shorter distribution channel actually change?
flashcards.back: How much of the price reaches the producer, and how much of the work it does. It does not automatically mean a lower price for the consumer — whether any margin is passed on is a separate decision.

flashcards.front: Why do longer channels still exist?
flashcards.back: Wholesalers and retailers do work the producer would otherwise pay for — holding stock, breaking bulk, reaching small buyers — and for a low-value product bought casually they do it more cheaply than the producer could.

flashcards.front: Name the main changes in distribution methods.
flashcards.back: Selling online; delivery instead of collection; supplying access rather than the object (subscriptions, streaming); and running several channels at once, which means competing with your own stockists.

chains.title: How a marketing objective becomes a price
steps: The business says which objective it is pursuing.
Share points at the lowest price it will accept; revenue points at $16; profit points at $20.
The pricing strategy is then chosen to reach that price.
The rest of the mix is set so the price is credible.
chains.result: A business that has not named its objective cannot price, because three objectives give three answers

chains.title: How building a brand reaches the price list
steps: Spending on USPs, advertising, sponsorship and social media builds what buyers expect of the name.
Demand becomes less sensitive to price: elasticity at $20 moves from −1.67 to −1.00.
A price rise now costs fewer sales, so $24 turns from a $640,000 outcome into $768,000.
The profit-maximising price moves from $20 to $24.
chains.result: Reduced price elasticity is the benefit; the premium price and the added value are its consequences

chains.title: How a stage in the life cycle chooses a pricing strategy
steps: At introduction the product is new and rivals have nothing like it, so skimming or penetration fits.
Through growth the early buyers run out and the price comes down in steps.
In maturity rivals are established and little separates the products, so pricing becomes competitive.
In decline the price is part of the choice between an extension strategy and withdrawal.
chains.result: Stage in the product life cycle is one of the six pricing factors because the right strategy changes as the product ages

chains.title: How a channel decision reaches the producer's margin
steps: Each stage buys from the one before and adds a mark-up: $10 → $12 → $19.20 on the four stage route.
The consumer pays $19.20 — the same as through the three stage route.
But the producer receives $10 rather than $12, so it keeps $2 instead of $4.
The longer route buys reach: a wholesaler supplies retailers the producer could never sell to one at a time.
chains.result: The channel decision is margin against reach, not a decision about what the consumer pays

chains.title: How easy price comparison changes what a business invests in
steps: Online sales and comparison sites cut the cost of comparing prices to almost nothing.
Substitutes become easy to find, so price elasticity of demand rises.
The room to hold a price above a rival's narrows, and competitive pricing becomes closer to automatic.
What a comparison site cannot sort on — a USP, a brand, a service — becomes the only place a gap can be held.
chains.result: Easier comparison raises the value of everything that is not price

mistakes.title: Treating Market Share and Revenue as the Same Objective
mistakes.mistake: Students write that a price cut which wins market share must also raise revenue, because more units were sold.
mistakes.correction: Revenue is price times quantity, and a price cut moves both — one up, one down. On this section's figures a business sells 100,000 bottles at $12 and 60,000 at $20, and the revenue is $1,200,000 either way. Market share is largest at the lowest price; revenue peaks at $16; profit peaks at $20. Three objectives, three prices.
mistakes.examTip: Work the multiplication before saying which way revenue went. If the question names an objective, say which price that objective points at, and whether the other objectives point somewhere else.

mistakes.title: Reading the Product Life Cycle as a Timetable
mistakes.mistake: Students write that a product "must" be in decline because it has been on sale for several years, or that maturity lasts a fixed period.
mistakes.correction: The cycle describes a pattern of sales, not a schedule. A fashion item can pass through all four stages in a season while a staple food stays in maturity for decades. A product is in the stage its sales say it is in, and the evidence is the direction sales are moving.
mistakes.examTip: Quote the sales figures in the extract before naming the stage. An answer that names a stage from the product's age has not used the data it was given.

mistakes.title: Withdrawing Every Dog
mistakes.mistake: Students see a product in the dog quadrant and recommend divesting it, every time, without looking at what it does for the business.
mistakes.correction: A dog may cover its own costs, complete a range a retailer insists on stocking, or matter to buyers the business wants to keep. It may also be a former cash cow whose market is still large. The matrix raises the question; it does not answer it.
mistakes.examTip: Say which case this dog is before recommending anything, and name what the business would lose by dropping it as well as what it would save.

mistakes.title: Listing the Marketing Mix Instead of Mixing It
mistakes.mistake: Students describe product, then promotion, then price, then place, one at a time, and never connect them — which is exactly what the word "mix" warns against.
mistakes.correction: A decision in one element constrains the other three. A premium product cannot be sold cheaply through a discount channel without the buyer reading the mismatch as a reason to distrust the claim. Asked to evaluate a marketing decision, the marks are in what the change FORCES elsewhere.
mistakes.examTip: After naming a change to one element, write one sentence on what each of the other three now has to be. That sentence is the difference between describing the mix and using it.

mistakes.title: Calling a Low Price a Unique Selling Point
mistakes.mistake: Students offer "it is the cheapest" as a USP, or as the differentiation factor in a pricing answer.
mistakes.correction: A price is the easiest thing in any market to match, and matching it costs a rival nothing but margin. A selling point holds only where copying it would cost something real — a guarantee that has to be honoured, a material that has to be sourced, a service that has to be staffed.
mistakes.examTip: Test any claimed USP by asking what it would cost a rival to copy it by the end of the month. If the answer is "nothing", it is not a selling point and it will not support a price.

mistakes.title: Believing a Brand Must Raise Sales
mistakes.mistake: Students write that a successful brand-building campaign will increase the number of units sold, and judge the campaign a failure if sales are flat.
mistakes.correction: A brand changes the SHAPE of demand rather than its level. On this section's figures both demand lines pass through the same $20 and the same 60,000 bottles — today's sales are identical. What changed is that the rise to $24 costs 8,000 fewer bottles than it would have without the brand — 12,000 lost rather than 20,000 — turning $640,000 of profit into $768,000.
mistakes.examTip: Judge brand spending by what happens when the price moves, not by this year's volume. A brand that lets a business hold a price rise has paid for itself without selling one extra unit.

mistakes.title: Thinking Cost Plus Guarantees a Profit
mistakes.mistake: Students write that cost plus pricing means the business cannot make a loss, because the mark-up is added to the cost.
mistakes.correction: Cost plus guarantees a margin on each sale that is MADE. Nothing in the arithmetic asks whether buyers will pay the price it produces: $8 at 150% gives $20 with exactly the same confidence as 50% gives $12. If the price is above what the market will pay, the margin is on nothing.
mistakes.examTip: When an answer recommends cost plus, say what would tell the business its mark-up was wrong. That is the weakness the method has, and naming it is what turns knowledge into evaluation.

mistakes.title: Assuming a Shorter Channel Means a Cheaper Product
mistakes.mistake: Students write that cutting out the wholesaler or the retailer passes the saving on to the consumer.
mistakes.correction: It passes more of the price to the PRODUCER. On this section's figures the four stage and three stage channels both reach the consumer at $19.20; what differs is whether the producer keeps $2 or $4. And the margin arrives with work attached — stock, payments, delivery and returns that the retailer used to absorb.
mistakes.examTip: Separate two questions: what the consumer pays, and who keeps it. A channel answer that only discusses the shelf price has answered the wrong one.
